The paper records the promotion-and-stacking theorems of Section 10 and the self-reference theorems of Section 11:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Promotion gate soundness} (Theorem 19) and \emph{strict promotion implies nonfactorization} (Theorem 20): any accepted-family promotion verdict requires every required core gate to exist and pass, and a strict promotion verdict implies a nonfactorization witness on the carrier.
\item
  \emph{Non-strict promotion implies factorization} (Theorem 21): a non-strict promotion verdict on an admissible bridge implies a factorization filler.
\item
  \emph{Toy strict bridge} (Example Theorem 22): a finite two-layer bridge witnesses the strict-promotion pattern without proving any general stacking-composition theorem.
\item
  \emph{No-overreading suppression} (Theorem 23, Section 11): no \(I\)-accepted claim depends on unbridged suppressed content.
\item
  \emph{Same-level self-audit failure} (Theorem 24, Section 11): an instrument \(I_{0}\) does not certify its own complete soundness; the verdict is \(\texttt{outside\_scope}\) or \(\texttt{undefined\_circular}\).
\item
  \emph{Finite rotating-audit theorem} (Theorem 25, Section 11): a finite stack \(\mathbb I_{\le N}\) admits a level-\(N+1\) extension instrument that audits the lower stack and accepts compliance iff the stack-audit defect is empty, while remaining non-final on its own soundness.
\end{itemize}

expanded_source_wording_tex:
\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Section 2} records preliminaries and scope: finite host mathematics, primitive labels and levels, claim strengths, status discipline, and the global nonclaim conventions.
\item
  \emph{Sections 3 and 4} define the finite audited calculus: the finite typed domain, the central object \(\mathbf{BirdInt}^{\mathrm{aud}}_{\mathrm{fin}}\) as a finite typed tuple, theory packages, instruments, source-of-truth records, audit records, visibility bridges, directed-cell records, pair-observable records, promotion bridges, and the per-cell profile schema.
\item
  \emph{Section 5} records the status and defect semantics: the seven status families, the per-component defect schemas, the visibility-defect family, and the classifier priority orders.
\item
  \emph{Sections 6--8} prove the finite theorem spine: the no-total-algebra theorem and the four core finite-interaction theorems (Section 6); the nine descent/packaging/completion/strictness theorems (Section 7); and the four cohomological no-drive theorems on graph-supported drive (Section 8).
\item
  \emph{Section 9} records the countermodel atlas in main-text form, with full sheets for CM\_1--CM\_6 and named pointers to CM\_7--CM\_12. The full twelve-countermodel atlas is recorded in Appendix C.
\item
  \emph{Section 10} records promotion and stacking: the promotion-bridge schema, the eight-gate machinery, the promotion-status consequences of the classifier, Theorems 19--21, the Toy22 strict-bridge example, and the stacking claims not proved.
\item
  \emph{Section 11} records instruments, visibility, and rotating audit: the instrument-indexed claim semantics, the classifier priority, the visibility/suppression discipline, the no-overreading theorem (Theorem 23), the same-level self-audit failure theorem (Theorem 24), the \(P_{6}\leftarrow P_{6}\) status separation, the rotating-audit chain and bridge, the finite rotating-audit theorem (Theorem 25), and the instrument-transfer rule.
\item
  \emph{Section 12} records the abstract-interpretation model family: the host data, the realized fragment \(P_{1}/P_{2}/P_{4}/P_{5}/P_{6}\), Theorems 26--28 (closure as packaging, descent as sound transformer, representability as fixedness), and Model Theorem 29.
\item
  \emph{Section 13} records the four scoped model realizations (PICA, Cantor strict-bridge, abstract interpretation, graph/cohomology), Model Theorems 33 and 34, the combined model-realization matrix, and the cross-model role-coverage observation.
\item
  \emph{Section 14} records the secondary high-structure semantics: the finite decorated double-category fragment and the recovery theorems 30--32 (descent-square recovery, completion-pasting recovery, strict extension as no-filler).
\item
  \emph{Section 15} records the Lean 4 validation artifact, the manifest-driven validator, and Proposition 35.
\item
  \emph{Section 16} records limitations, nonclaims, and future work, with the final paper-inclusion nonclaim block of thirty-six entries.
\item
  \emph{Section 17} records the conclusion.
\item
  \emph{Appendices A--H} record the long-form supplementary material: full definitions and tables (A), long proofs (B), the full countermodel atlas (C), the four model-realization sheets (D), the high-structure semantics extension (E), the Lean mechanization appendix (F), the dependency graph (G), and the deferred and dropped claims register (H).
\end{itemize}

expanded_source_wording_tex:
\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\mathbb P\) is the fixed finite set of primitive labels \(\{P_1,\ldots,P_6\}\) defined in Subsection 2.2.1. It is the underlying label alphabet of every role-channel, directed-cell, pair-observable, promotion, and dependency judgment.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Lev}=\{\mathsf{Beh},\mathsf{Ver},\mathsf{Str}\}\) is the finite level set defined in Subsection 2.2.3, used to tag the kind of content a judgment refers to and to gate cross-level claims through translation, lift, forgetting, or reflection bridges.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Host}\) is the finite inventory of permitted hosts declared in Subsection 2.1.2: \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{fin}}\), \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{prob}}\), \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{graph}}\), \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{AI}}\), \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{PICA}}\), \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{CantorShell}}\), \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{DC}}\), \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{instr}}\). Every theorem statement names its host.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Cont}\) is the finite content universe of the domain, defined in Subsection 3.2. It collects the records that claims may use: theory packages, instruments, witnesses, updates, profiles, defect records, threshold records, audit records, visibility records, level/lens/interface records, package and promotion interfaces, quotients, lenses, completion endomaps, kernels, graphs, finite families, refinements, and other finite typed records introduced as the calculus is built.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Instr}\) is the finite family of instrument records, defined in Subsection 3.4. An instrument fixes the visible/suppressed map, scope, claim types, threshold and audit policies, level assignment, bridge policy, source policy, and nonclaim list under which a claim is to be evaluated.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Pkg}\) is the finite family of theory packages, defined in Subsection 3.3, each carrying the inherited Foundations I package data \((Z,f,\Sigma_f,E,\mathcal A)\) together with the additional Foundations III typed records (visibility, source, defect, promotion, model-realization) attached around it.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Prof}\) is the finite family of profile records, defined in Subsection 3.6. A profile fixes per-judgment data such as actor and informant level tags, scale, regime, bridge type, instrument mode, and locality, and is required by every directed-cell, pair-observable, promotion, and claim judgment.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Wit}\) assigns to each primitive \(P_i\in\mathbb P\) its typed witness family \(\mathsf{Wit}(P_i)\), defined in Subsection 3.7. The informant-side data of a directed cell is required to belong to one of these families.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Upd}\) assigns to each primitive \(P_i\in\mathbb P\) its typed update family \(\mathsf{Upd}(P_i)\), defined in Subsection 3.7. The actor-side data of a directed cell is required to belong to one of these families.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Def}\) is the finite family of defect records, defined in Section 5. A defect record carries a defect type, a domain, a witness, a threshold, a measured value, a status consequence, and an audit/source record, and feeds the defect-to-status rules of Subsection 5.6.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Judg}\) is the finite family of judgment forms used by the calculus: role-channel, directed-cell, pair-observable, promotion, dependency, and instrument-indexed claim judgments, all defined in Section 4.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Status}\) is the finite family of status sets, one per judgment family: role-channel, directed-cell, pair-observable, promotion, claim, gate, and square statuses. The sets are listed in Subsection 2.3.2 and defined fully in Section 5.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Gate}\) is the finite family of gate specifications used during promotion and claim acceptance, defined in Section 10. A gate is a finite check whose \(\texttt{pass}\), \(\texttt{fail}\), \(\texttt{not\_required}\), \(\texttt{not\_checked}\), or \(\texttt{outside\_scope}\) result feeds promotion-status and claim-status decisions.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Dep}\) is the finite family of dependency relations between primitives, including positive dependencies, blocked dependencies, bridge-required dependencies, and countermodel-supported no-go dependencies, defined in Subsection 4.6.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Audit}\) is the finite family of audit records, defined in Subsection 4.8. An audit record carries a target, an instrument, replay or check data, and admissibility data; it is distinct from the inherited audit functional \(\mathcal A\) that lives inside a theory package \(\mathcal T\).
\item
  \(\mathsf{Vis}\) is the finite family of visibility maps and visibility bridges, defined in Subsection 3.5. A visibility map sends content to one of \(\texttt{visible}\), \(\texttt{suppressed}\), \(\texttt{outside}\), \(\texttt{unknown}\) under an instrument, and a visibility bridge is the admissible record by which a claim may use suppressed content.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Source}\) is the finite family of source records, defined in Subsection 4.8. A source record fixes source identity, source type, trace, and source validity, and is consulted by pair-observable and claim acceptance rules.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Nonclaim}\) is the finite family of nonclaim records carried by an instrument or attached to a judgment. A nonclaim records what the surrounding statement does not assert, in the same finite typed format as the rest of the calculus.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Real}\) is the finite family of model-realization modules, defined in Section 13: the PICA, audited Cantor shell, abstract-interpretation, and graph/cohomology realizations of named fragments of the calculus.
\end{itemize}

conclusion: suppression is a relation between a record and an instrument, not a property of the record alone, and it does not assert that the suppressed record is false.
expanded_source_wording_tex:
\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Host.} Each record carries a host tag drawn from \(\mathsf{Host}\). The host tag fixes which finite mathematical universe the record lives in: \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{fin}}\) for the base host, \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{prob}}\) for finite stochastic content, \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{graph}}\) for finite graph and cohomology content, \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{AI}}\) for finite abstract-interpretation content, \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{PICA}}\) and \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{CantorShell}}\) for the model-realization hosts, \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{DC}}\) for the high-structure fragment, and \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{instr}}\) for instrument-side content.
\item
  \textbf{Level.} Each record carries a level tag drawn from \(\mathsf{Lev}=\{\mathsf{Beh},\mathsf{Ver},\mathsf{Str}\}\). The level tag fixes whether the record describes behavioral/trace content, verification/audit content, or structural/object content. A judgment that uses records at more than one level is admissible only with an explicit level bridge (translation, lift, forgetting, or reflection).
\item
  \textbf{Instrument.} Each record is interpreted under the instrument \(I\) that the surrounding judgment names. The instrument fixes whether the record is visible, suppressed, outside-scope, or unknown for the purpose of the claim, and what bridges may connect it to visible content. A record may be in \(\mathsf{Cont}\) globally and yet be suppressed under a particular instrument; suppression is a relation between a record and an instrument, not a property of the record alone, and it does not assert that the suppressed record is false.
\item
  \textbf{Profile.} Each judgment is tagged by a profile \(\lambda\in\mathsf{Prof}\) which fixes per-judgment data including actor and informant level tags, scale, regime, bridge type, instrument mode, and locality. The profile of a judgment together with its host, level, and instrument tags determines the admissibility of every record in its use-set.
\end{itemize}

conclusion: N_I : the finite nonclaim record of I .
expanded_source_wording_tex:
\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\mathrm{id}_I\): a finite identifier under which the instrument is registered. Two distinct instruments have distinct identifiers, and an instrument identifier is part of the data of every claim accepted under that instrument.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Scope}_I\): the finite scope record of the instrument, fixing the host, level, and content classes that fall inside its scope. A claim whose use-set is not contained in \(\mathsf{Scope}_I\) has status \(\texttt{outside\_scope}\) under \(I\).
\item
  \(\mathsf{ClaimTypes}_I\): the finite family of claim types that \(I\) is configured to evaluate, including role-channel, directed-cell, pair-observable, promotion, dependency, and instrument-indexed claim types as appropriate.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Visible}_I,\;\mathsf{Suppressed}_I\): the finite visibility partition of \(\mathsf{Scope}_I\) into visible and suppressed content under \(I\). The complement of \(\mathsf{Visible}_I\cup\mathsf{Suppressed}_I\) within \(\mathsf{Scope}_I\) is the unknown class; content outside \(\mathsf{Scope}_I\) is in the outside-scope class. The full four-way partition is given in Subsection 3.5.
\item
  \(\mathsf{CheckRules}_I\): the finite family of check rules used to classify a claim under \(I\). Check rules are typed finite records: each rule states which fields of a claim it consults, what comparison or test it performs, and what classifier verdict it contributes.
\item
  \(\mathsf{EvidencePolicy}_I\): the finite policy for what counts as admissible evidence under \(I\), distinguishing direct evidence, bridge-relayed evidence, and inadmissible evidence.
\item
  \(\mathsf{ThresholdPolicy}_I\): the finite family of thresholds used by \(I\), including exact, approximate, tolerance, rank/dimension, visibility, and source thresholds. The threshold record schema is fixed in Subsection 5.2.
\item

\item

\end{itemize}

conclusion: Nonclaims : the nonclaim records required by the audited claim or object.
expanded_source_wording_tex:
\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\mathsf{ClaimRef}\): a finite reference to the object or claim being audited. Targets include theory packages, directed cells, pair observables, promotion bridges, instrument-indexed claim records, dependency records, and source records.
\item
  \(\mathsf{EvidenceRefs}\): the finite evidence references consulted by the audit.
\item
  \(\mathsf{CheckRules}\): the finite check rules, including the instrument and audit policy under which the audit is performed. An audit record without an instrumented check policy is malformed.
\item
  \(\mathsf{CheckResults}\): the finite replay or check results produced by applying the check rules.
\item
  \(\mathsf{SourceRefs}\): the source records used by the audited claim or object.
\item
  \(\mathsf{VisibilityCheck}\): the finite visibility check against the named instrument's visibility map and bridge policy.
\item
  \(\mathsf{ThresholdCheck}\): the finite threshold check against the relevant threshold record.
\item
  \(\mathsf{CircularityCheck}\): the check that no unstratified circular audit/support loop occurs.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Nonclaims}\): the nonclaim records required by the audited claim or object.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Provenance}\): the finite provenance trace of the audit record.
\end{itemize}

expanded_source_wording_tex:
\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\mathbb P=\{P_1,\ldots,P_6\}\) is the fixed finite primitive set of Subsection 2.2.1.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Lev}=\{\mathsf{Beh},\mathsf{Ver},\mathsf{Str}\}\) is the fixed finite level set of Subsection 2.2.3.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Host}\) is a finite subfamily of the host inventory of Subsection 2.1.2; only hosts named in \(\mathsf{Host}\) may appear on the host tag of any record in the instance.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Cont}\) is the finite content universe of the instance (Subsection 3.2): finite typed records, each with a host tag from \(\mathsf{Host}\), a level tag from \(\mathsf{Lev}\), an instrument-relative visibility class drawn from Subsection 3.5, and a profile attachment when required.
\item
  All references among content records resolve, or else the missing reference is represented by an explicit absence record in the appropriate status family.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Instr}\) is a finite family of admissible instruments, each meeting the conditions of Subsection 3.4.1.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Pkg}\) is a finite family of admissible theory packages, each meeting the conditions of Subsection 3.3.3.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Prof}\) is a finite family of admissible profiles, each meeting the conditions of Subsection 3.6.2.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Wit}\) and \(\mathsf{Upd}\) are the witness and update maps of Subsection 3.7.1-3.7.2; their values on each \(P_i\) are finite typed families, with the actor/informant typing rule \(W_j\in\mathsf{Wit}(P_j)\), \(U_i\in\mathsf{Upd}(P_i)\) enforced on every directed-cell record.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Def}\) is a finite family of admissible defect records in the schema of Subsection 5.2.1.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Judg}\) is the finite family of judgment forms introduced in Subsections 4.2 through 4.7 (role-channel, directed-cell, pair-observable, promotion, dependency, instrument-indexed claim).
\item
  \(\mathsf{Status}\) is the finite family of status sets associated to those judgment forms (role, cell, pair, promotion, claim, gate, square), listed in Subsection 5.1.
\item
  Threshold records are finite and typed in the threshold schema of Subsection 5.2.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Gate}\) is the finite family of gate specifications used in Sections 10 and 11, with the gate status sets \(\mathrm{GateStatus}\) and \(\mathrm{StrictGateStatus}\) from Subsection 5.1.6; promotion gates are explicit whenever a promotion judgment is claimed.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Dep}\) is a finite family of admissible dependency records in the schema of Subsection 4.6.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Audit}\) and \(\mathsf{Source}\) are finite families of admissible audit and source records in the schemas of Subsections 4.8.2 and 4.8.1.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Vis}\) is the finite family of visibility maps and visibility bridges of Subsection 3.5.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Nonclaim}\) is a finite family of admissible nonclaim records, attached either to instruments (as \(\mathcal N_I\)) or to individual judgments.
\item
  \(\mathsf{Real}\) is a finite family of admissible model-realization modules; admissibility of a model-realization module is the schema fixed in Section 13.
\end{itemize}

expanded_source_wording_tex: Directed cells \(P_i\leftarrow P_j\) are typed bridge judgments, not primitive products. The notation is closed against algebraic interpretation: there is no underlying multiplication of primitives whose values can determine cell status, and the typed witness, update, profile, level, visibility, threshold, audit, and defect data carried by every cell record are essential for the classifier's verdict. NC-1 of Subsection 2.4.3 is the corresponding nonclaim. Subsequent sections of this paper use directed-cell records, not primitive-pair labels, as the working unit of typed interaction; in particular, Section 13's PICA model-realization sheet does not interpret the \(6\times 6\) table as a universal interaction algebra.

The record constructor permits distinct primitive labels, for example \(P_1\leftarrow P_5\) for descent through a package or \(P_3\leftarrow P_5\) for noncommuting completions, with witness data drawn from the informant family and update data drawn from the actor family. Hence active interaction does not entail \(P_i=P_j\).

conclusion: Pair labels alone do not determine cell status. The same primitive pair (P_i,P_j) , with different witness, update, profile, threshold, visibility, audit, or defect data, can produce different cell statuses; this was the working content of Theorem 1, and Theorem 2 records the underlying typed-record discipline that licenses it. No theorem in this paper infers the equality of two primitive labels from the existence of a directed-cell judgment between them; in particular, no theorem in Sections 7, 10, or 13 does so even when the cell receives status action .

expanded_source_wording_tex: The gate-results record \(\mathsf{GateResults}(B)\) is the finite assignment of these statuses to the gates in the bridge record. A gate may be marked \(\texttt{not\_required}\) when the bridge does not claim the corresponding content; the descent gate, for example, is \(\texttt{not\_required}\) for a bridge that records only an interface change with no closure claim. A required core gate marked \(\texttt{not\_checked}\) does not yield an accepted promotion; the promotion classifier of Subsection 5.6.4 routes such a bridge to \(\texttt{candidate}\).

conclusion: The order encodes the intended discipline: an outside-scope claim is recorded outside scope rather than rejected
expanded_source_wording_tex: A claim record matching multiple per-status conditions is assigned the highest-priority match. The order encodes the intended discipline: an outside-scope claim is recorded outside scope rather than rejected; a claim whose use-set contains suppressed unbridged content is blocked rather than rejected; audited absence and failed audits are recorded before threshold or refutation outcomes; circularity is recorded once the earlier scope, visibility, source, and audit checks do not already determine the status; and the accepted verdict is the lowest-priority match, reached only when every higher condition has been ruled out.

conclusion: This subsection records the finite rotating-audit theorem of Foundations III. expanded_source_wording_tex: \emph{Admissibility of the bridge.} Each clause of \(\mathsf{AdmRotAuditBridge}\bigl(B^{\mathrm{audit}}_{\le N\to N+1}\bigr)\) of Subsection 11.7.3 is verified on the finite records: clause (1) is the admissibility of the source instruments and of \(I_{N+1}^{\mathrm{stack}}\); clause (2) is the strict level inequality fixed by construction; clause (3) is the finite declaration of \(\Phi_{\le N}\); clause (4) is satisfied because \(I_{N+1}^{\mathrm{stack}}\)'s scope contains \(\mathsf{Target}_{\le N}\); clause (5) is the language map; clauses (6)--(9) are the visibility, threshold, audit, and defect-typing requirements built into the construction; clause (10) is the no-unstratified-same-level-cycle requirement, satisfied because the audit dependency graph points strictly upward, from level \(\le N\) to level \(N+1\); clause (11) is the nonclaim presence. conclusion: This is the model-realization nonclaim of Subsection 2.4. This is the model-coverage nonclaim of Subsection 13.6.
expanded_source_wording_tex:
\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Fragment-only realization.} A model-realization statement \(\mathcal M\models\mathcal S:\texttt{model\_realization}\) asserts realization of \(\mathcal S\) and not of the whole calculus. The verdict \(\texttt{model\_realization}\) for \(\mathcal S\) does not imply a \(\texttt{model\_realization}\) verdict for any larger fragment \(\mathcal S'\supsetneq\mathcal S\).
\item
  \emph{No theorem grade by realization.} A model-realization verdict is not a theorem-grade verdict. In the absence of a separately admissible theorem-grade bridge, \(\mathcal M\models\mathcal S:\texttt{model\_realization}\) does not yield a \(\texttt{accepted}\) verdict on a theorem-grade claim about \(\mathcal S\). This is the model-realization nonclaim of Subsection 2.4.
\item
  \emph{Host-bound realization.} A model-realization verdict for \(\mathcal S\) under \(\mathcal M\) is bound to the host of \(\mathcal M\): it does not transfer to other hosts without an admissible instrument-transfer bridge in the sense of Subsection 11.9.
\item
  \emph{No model-coverage theorem.} The four realizations recorded in Subsections 13.2--13.4 and Section 12 do not, taken together, support a global model-coverage theorem for \(\mathbf{BirdInt}^{\mathrm{aud}}_{\mathrm{fin}}\). This is the model-coverage nonclaim of Subsection 13.6.
\end{itemize}

conclusion: The PICA nonclaim register N_ PICA contains, in particular: enumi . enumi . PICA is not the universal six-bird algebra: PICAReal_ fin realizes a declared finite stochastic fragment, not the whole calculus. The recovered 6× 6 multiplicity count is a PICA-profile model fact under the cell profile lambda_ PICA , not a universal 6× 6 law. Raw PICA status is not formal status without recovery and classifier check; the formal classifier verdict is the authoritative cell status. Directed-cell status action does not imply pair-realness; pair-realness requires the source/visibility/audit/threshold conjunction of Subsubsection 13.2.7. A fallback record does not by itself support a real pair source-of-truth; it supports at most real_provisional . Ablation evidence in Abl is model-realization evidence, not theorem-grade evidence, in the absence of an admissible bridge to a theorem-grade claim. A P_3 route mismatch is not a P6_ drive assertion in the sense of Section 8: the two are connected only through an admissible drive bridge. A dirty record cannot support a real claim under any host configuration of H_ PICA . PICA realizes a finite stochastic fragment, and not the entirety of BirdInt^ aud _ fin ; this restates the fragment discipline of Subsection 13.1.2. Implementation correctness of any concrete PICA implementation is future work and is not certified by this realization theorem; the Lean validation record of Section 15 is a separate, manifest-scoped artifact.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\arabic{enumi}.{\arabic{enumi}.}

\item

\item

\item
  PICA realizes a finite stochastic fragment, and not the entirety of \(\mathbf{BirdInt}^{\mathrm{aud}}_{\mathrm{fin}}\); this restates the fragment discipline of Subsection 13.1.2.
\item
  Implementation correctness of any concrete PICA implementation is future work and is not certified by this realization theorem; the Lean validation record of Section 15 is a separate, manifest-scoped artifact.
\end{enumerate}

conclusion: The Cantor nonclaim register N_ Cantor contains: enumi . enumi . The realization is scoped to the audited Cantor shell S_ aud ; it is not a shell-general theorem and does not assert a strict-bridge passage outside the shell. There is no shell-general strict-bridge theorem; extending the realization beyond S_ aud requires a separately admissible bridge. There is no broader external-class theorem; the realization does not assert structural facts about external classes of theories unless an admissible inter-theory bridge is supplied. Strictness does not imply macro closure: the strictness witness of Subsubsection 13.3.5 is object-map nonfactorization, not closure of macro dynamics. Strictness does not imply drive: the realization does not supply a P6_ drive assertion in the sense of Section 8 without a separately admissible drive bridge. The pressure-gap consequence defect of Subsubsection 13.3.6 is not a Kullback–Leibler closure deficit unless an admissible bridge to the KL closure-deficit framework is recorded. The pressure-gap defect is not the strictness witness; it is a consequence of the witness, recorded as a separate defect record. The pressure-gap functional Delta_ T_0→ T_1 is a conditional pressure disintegration on the persistent strata family F , and is not a direct stratumwise root separation. Cantor is a model realization/application, not a universal strict-extension theory. The target completion T_1 is not merely repeated application of one fixed idempotent completion; it is the packaged completion of Subsubsection 13.3.3.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\arabic{enumi}.{\arabic{enumi}.}

\item
  The drive certificate \(\mathrm{P6}_{\mathrm{drive}}^{H^1}\) with \([a]\neq 0\) in \(H^{1}(G;k)\) is one drive certificate family, not every possible drive notion.

\item
  The condition \(H^{1}(G;k)=0\) is a no-drive certificate for cohomological drive on \(G\), and not a no-drive certificate for any other notion of activity.
\item
  Nonzero route holonomy on \(G\) can coexist with a zero drive cochain \(a\); the two are distinct records.

  The graph/cohomology host \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{graph}}\) is finite and scoped; it is not a universal cohomological framework.

\item

\item
  Positive holonomy-to-drive claims --- that a positive route holonomy implies a positive drive --- require an admissible drive bridge \(B_{3\to 6}^{\mathrm{drive}}\) in the sense of Section 8.
\end{enumerate}

The paper records twelve finite countermodels, each blocking a specific overclaim about the calculus: active package without macro closure (CM\_1), active route/holonomy without drive (CM\_2), local packages failing globally (CM\_3), directed cell active while the pair observable is blocked (CM\_4), refinement worsening closure (CM\_5), same-level self-audit circularity (CM\_6), same primitive pair with different statuses (CM\_7), idempotent completions that do not commute (CM\_8), strict extension without macro closure (CM\_9), strict extension without drive (CM\_10), fallback source unable to support a real pair observable (CM\_11), and gating that destroys cycle-supported drive (CM\_12).

Each countermodel is a finite typed structure under an instrument whose visible content blocks the corresponding overclaim under \(I\). The atlas is finite, audited, and host-bound, in keeping with the no-go scope discipline of Subsection 9.1.

The non-factorization of cell status through the primitive pair (Theorem 1, Section 6) blocks any such operation as a status-decoding map. No all-mathematics reduction. The paper does not assert that all mathematics is six birds, or that every mathematical object is a BirdInt^ aud _ fin object under any reading. No unrestricted exact-six theorem. The paper does not assert that every typed interaction is exactly representable as one of the thirty-six directed cells P_ i P_ j . The exact-six structure is recorded as a finite typed schema with admissibility conditions, not as an unrestricted decomposition theorem. No unique decomposition. The paper does not assert that a typed interaction has a unique decomposition into primitive directed cells. Decomposition records are admissible only under a declared profile and audit, and different profiles can yield different admissible decompositions.

\item
  \emph{No unique decomposition.} The paper does not assert that a typed interaction has a unique decomposition into primitive directed cells. Decomposition records are admissible only under a declared profile and audit, and different profiles can yield different admissible decompositions.
\end{itemize}

conclusion: No audit-is-truth. The paper does not assert that a claim status accepted under instrument I is instrument-free truth. The instrument-indexed claim form of Subsection 11.1.3 fixes acceptance as relative to I and the surrounding context Gamma; T . No same-level complete self-certification. The paper does not assert that a single instrument I_ 0 certifies its own complete soundness. Theorem 24 of Section 11 records the formal failure: same-level complete self-soundness is either outside_scope or undefined_circular under I_ 0 . No rotating-audit finality. Theorem 25 of Section 11 and the non-finality clause of Subsubsection 11.8.3 record that a finite rotating-audit chain audits the lower stack but does not certify its top. No accepted claim overreads hidden content. The paper does not assert that an accepted claim under I implies any fact about I -suppressed content. Theorem 23 of Section 11 records the formal no-overreading result.

\tightlist
\item
  \emph{No audit-is-truth.} The paper does not assert that a claim status \(\texttt{accepted}\) under instrument \(I\) is instrument-free truth. The instrument-indexed claim form of Subsection 11.1.3 fixes acceptance as relative to \(I\) and the surrounding context \(\Gamma;\mathcal T\).
\item
  \emph{No same-level complete self-certification.} The paper does not assert that a single instrument \(I_{0}\) certifies its own complete soundness. Theorem 24 of Section 11 records the formal failure: same-level complete self-soundness is either \(\texttt{outside\_scope}\) or \(\texttt{undefined\_circular}\) under \(I_{0}\).
\item
  \emph{No rotating-audit finality.} The paper does not assert that a finite rotating-audit chain is final. Theorem 25 of Section 11 and the non-finality clause of Subsubsection 11.8.3 record that a finite rotating-audit chain audits the lower stack but does not certify its top.
\item
  \emph{No accepted claim overreads hidden content.} The paper does not assert that an accepted claim under \(I\) implies any fact about \(I\)-suppressed content. Theorem 23 of Section 11 records the formal no-overreading result.
\end{itemize}

conclusion: The paper records its earned content as a layered theorem stack: Finite typed calculus and core theorems. Sections 6 and 7 record the no-total-algebra theorem (Theorem 1), the four core finite-interaction theorems (Theorems 2–5), and the nine descent/packaging/completion/strictness theorems (Theorems 6–14), all theorem-grade with verdict accepted . No-go and cohomological theorems. Section 8 records the four cohomological no-drive theorems (Theorems 15–18) on graph-supported drive. Countermodel/no-go atlas. Section 9 and Appendix C record twelve countermodels (CM_1–CM_12), each blocking a specific overclaim about the calculus under a finite typed structure. Promotion and instrument-indexed semantics. Section 10 records the promotion gate and strictness theorems (Theorems 19–21) together with the Toy22 strict-bridge example (Theorem 22), and Section 11 records the no-overreading suppression theorem (Theorem 23), the same-level self-audit failure theorem (Theorem 24), and the finite rotating-audit theorem (Theorem 25), each accompanied by the finite typed instrument-indexed claim form. Scoped model realizations. Section 12 records theorem-grade abstract-interpretation host results (Theorems 26–28) and the model-grade abstract-interpretation family result (Model Theorem 29). Section 13 records the PICA realization (Model Theorem 33), the Cantor strict-bridge realization (Model Theorem 34), and the graph/cohomology realization, all model-grade with verdict model_realization on declared fragments. High-structure semantics as secondary organization. Section 14 records three decorated-square recovery theorems (Theorems 30–32) over a finite double-category fragment, presented as secondary organization rather than as a replacement for the core calculus. Lean validation audit. Section 15 records the manifest-scoped Lean 4 validation artifact and Proposition 35, with the audit-grade verdict audit_report .

The paper records its earned content as a layered theorem stack:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Finite typed calculus and core theorems.} Sections 6 and 7 record the no-total-algebra theorem (Theorem 1), the four core finite-interaction theorems (Theorems 2--5), and the nine descent/packaging/completion/strictness theorems (Theorems 6--14), all theorem-grade with verdict \(\texttt{accepted}\).
\item
  \emph{No-go and cohomological theorems.} Section 8 records the four cohomological no-drive theorems (Theorems 15--18) on graph-supported drive.
\item
  \emph{Countermodel/no-go atlas.} Section 9 and Appendix C record twelve countermodels (CM\_1--CM\_12), each blocking a specific overclaim about the calculus under a finite typed structure.
\item
  \emph{Promotion and instrument-indexed semantics.} Section 10 records the promotion gate and strictness theorems (Theorems 19--21) together with the Toy22 strict-bridge example (Theorem 22), and Section 11 records the no-overreading suppression theorem (Theorem 23), the same-level self-audit failure theorem (Theorem 24), and the finite rotating-audit theorem (Theorem 25), each accompanied by the finite typed instrument-indexed claim form.
\item
  \emph{Scoped model realizations.} Section 12 records theorem-grade abstract-interpretation host results (Theorems 26--28) and the model-grade abstract-interpretation family result (Model Theorem 29). Section 13 records the PICA realization (Model Theorem 33), the Cantor strict-bridge realization (Model Theorem 34), and the graph/cohomology realization, all model-grade with verdict \(\texttt{model\_realization}\) on declared fragments.
\item
  \emph{High-structure semantics as secondary organization.} Section 14 records three decorated-square recovery theorems (Theorems 30--32) over a finite double-category fragment, presented as secondary organization rather than as a replacement for the core calculus.
\item
  \emph{Lean validation audit.} Section 15 records the manifest-scoped Lean 4 validation artifact and Proposition 35, with the audit-grade verdict \(\texttt{audit\_report}\).
\end{itemize}

source_wording_digest: Host , the finite and scoped host inventory, recording finite carriers, finite maps, finite records, finite relations, finite diagrams, finite graphs, and finite audit records (Subsection 2.1); Cont , the finite content set whose records may be visible, suppressed, outside-scope, or unknown under an instrument (Subsections 3.2 and 3.5); P=\ P_ 1 ,P_ 2 ,P_ 3 ,P_ 4 ,P_ 5 ,P_ 6 \ , the finite primitive labels with stable role glosses (Subsection 2.2); Lev , the finite level set \ Beh,Ver,Str\ used by the calculus (Subsection 2.2.3); Instr , the finite class of instrument records, with components introduced in Subsection 3.4 and used in the claim semantics of Subsection 11.1; Pkg , the finite class of theory packages with components (Z,f,Sigma_ f ,E, A) (Subsection 3.3); Prof , the finite typed profile family lambda with admissibility predicates (Subsection 3.6); Wit , the finite typed witness family for primitive informants (Subsection 3.7 and Table A.2); Upd , the finite typed update family for primitive actors (Subsection 3.7 and Table A.3); Def , the finite typed defect family with per-component schemas (Subsections 5.2 through 5.5 and Table A.6); Judg , the finite typed judgment family — role-channel, directed-cell, pair-observable, promotion, claim, gate, square — with per-judgment admissibility predicates (Subsections 4.2 through 4.7, 10.2, 11.1, and 14.1); Status , the seven finite status families, with their family-specific classifier and priority rules where defined (Subsection 5.1 and Table A.5); Gate , the finite typed gate family — eight promotion gates, the strict-pass gate, and bridge-admissibility gates (Subsection 10.2); Dep , the finite dependency record, recording producer/consumer relations among store entries and the dependency-graph schema (Subsection 4.6); Audit , the finite typed audit family — host audit, claim audit, bridge audit, rotating-audit (Subsection 4.8 and Section 11); Nonclaim , the finite nonclaim register N (Subsection 16.4 and per-record nonclaim subfields throughout).

\emph{Statement (recall).} Let \(G\rightsquigarrow G'=(V',E')\) be a \(P_{2}\)-gating that sends \(G\) to a forest, that is, \(\beta_{1}(G')=0\). Then \(H^{1}(G';k)=0\), and the cycle-supported cohomological drive certificate \(\mathrm{P6}_{\mathrm{drive}}^{H^1}\) is absent-with-record on \(G'\).

\emph{Proof.} By the forest no-drive theorem (Subsubsection B.2.1), \(\beta_{1}(G')=0\) implies \(H^{1}(G';k)=0\). Hence every cohomology class on \(G'\) is zero; in particular, the restriction \([a|_{G'}]\) is the zero class in \(H^{1}(G';k)\), so the drive certificate \(\kappa_{6}^{\mathrm{drive}}(a)\) does not survive the gating \(G\rightsquigarrow G'\).

conclusion: Theorem 1 of Section 6 records the formal counterexample, and NC-1 of Subsection 16.4 records the corresponding nonclaim. NC-2 of Subsection 16.4 records the corresponding nonclaim. The dropped claim is recorded in Subsubsection 1.3.2 and the corresponding nonclaim in NC-1 and the algebra/universality grouping of Subsubsection 16.2.1. expanded_source_wording_tex:
\begin{enumerate}
\def\arabic{enumi}.{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Universal six-symbol algebra.} No total operation \(\ast:\mathbb P^{2}\to\mathbb P\) recovers cell status across profiles. Theorem 1 of Section 6 records the formal counterexample, and \(\mathrm{NC}\text{-}1\) of Subsection 16.4 records the corresponding nonclaim.
\item
  \textbf{All mathematics is six birds.} The claim that every mathematical structure decomposes into the six primitives is dropped; \(\mathbf{BirdInt}^{\mathrm{aud}}_{\mathrm{fin}}\) is a finite typed audited interaction calculus, not a foundation for all mathematics. \(\mathrm{NC}\text{-}2\) of Subsection 16.4 records the corresponding nonclaim.
\item
  \textbf{Unrestricted exact-six.} The unrestricted decomposition claim, that every typed interaction is exactly representable as one of the thirty-six directed cells, is dropped. The exact-six structure is a finite typed schema with admissibility conditions, not an unrestricted decomposition theorem. The dropped claim is recorded in Subsubsection 1.3.2 and the corresponding nonclaim in \(\mathrm{NC}\text{-}1\) and the algebra/universality grouping of Subsubsection 16.2.1.
\item
  \textbf{PICA as canonical algebra.} The claim that PICA defines the canonical \(6\times 6\) algebra of the calculus is dropped. PICA is a finite stochastic model realization, scoped to the cell/pair/provenance fragment, and the recovered \(6\times 6\) multiplicity count is a profile fact, not a universal law. PICA nonclaims 1 and 2 of Subsubsection 13.2.10 and \(\mathrm{NC}\text{-}20\), \(\mathrm{NC}\text{-}21\) of Subsection 16.4 record the corresponding nonclaims.
\item
  \textbf{Cantor pressure gap as unbridged strictness witness.} The claim that the pressure-gap defect \(\Delta_{T_{0}\to T_{1}}\) is itself the strictness witness, rather than a consequence of the strictness witness, is dropped. The strictness witness is the factorization defect \(\Delta_{\mathrm{fact}}^{\mathrm{Cantor}}\); the pressure-gap defect is recorded as a consequence record. Cantor nonclaim 7 of Subsubsection 13.3.9 and \(\mathrm{NC}\text{-}27\) of Subsection 16.4 record the corresponding nonclaim.
\item
  \textbf{Provenance as proof.} The claim that provenance records constitute proof of any underlying mathematical fact is dropped. Provenance records are finite typed records of producer, source, audit, and visibility data; they support pair-realness and source-of-truth predicates but are not theorem-grade proofs of mathematical claims. The audit nonclaim \(\mathrm{NC}\text{-}15\) of Subsection 16.4 (no audit-is-truth) records the corresponding boundary.
\item
  \textbf{High-structure semantics as replacement calculus.} The claim that the finite decorated double-category fragment of Section 14 replaces or supersedes the core calculus is dropped. The decorated-square fragment is a secondary organizational layer; it records three specific recoveries (Theorems 30--32) and not a general claim that every theorem-grade fact reduces to a decorated-square fact. \(\mathrm{NC}\text{-}34\), \(\mathrm{NC}\text{-}35\) of Subsection 16.4 record the corresponding nonclaims.
\end{enumerate}

conclusion: Foundations IV is a catalog of layer-agnostic structural laws built on the Foundations I/II/III apparatus. Its organizing question is what must be true, before choosing a substrate—whether analysis, arithmetic, physics, biology, chemistry, economics and finance, linguistics, cognitive and social science, or computation—for a layer to have lawful access, stable records, transport, symmetry, closure, and limits. The contribution is a uniform normal-form template applied across 52 laws; each row states its setup, theorem, proof spine, case structure, interaction status, and nonclaims, so recurring obstructions such as failed descent, hidden predictive structure, local-global failure, and record nonclosure can be compared in one register. The formalization status is explicit: the catalog contains 46 direct Lean theorems, 2 substrate-delegated anchors (No-Needles Stability and Closure–Reality Boundary), 2 partial wrappers (Hiddenness and Duality Fixity), and 2 obligation wrappers (CSL Formed-Closure and Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking); the four trust-base axioms used by the wrappers are disclosed through an opacity-guard pattern, each guarded by an opaque source predicate that prevents the axiom from being instantiated without the corresponding substrate or future-source certificate. Foundations IV is not a foundational reset of Foundations I/II/III, not a unification claim about the eight axes, and not an exhaustive catalog.

expanded_source_wording_tex:
The example is intentionally elementary.  It uses no special
operator theory, no hidden regularity hypothesis, and no category
larger than the quotient construction itself.  Nevertheless, the
same shape appears in more elaborate settings.  A local family may
agree on overlaps but fail to come from a global object.  A symmetric
construction may be unable to choose a non-fixed branch without
adding symmetry-breaking data.  A formally closed record may exist
without being physically instantiated.  A finite observation may
determine all declared future probes, or fail precisely because some
future probe separates states the present quotient cannot see.  In
each case there is a setup, an obstruction, a repair or boundary, and
a statement of what the theorem does not claim.  The purpose of this
paper is to put those repeated shapes into a common register.

expanded_source_wording_tex:
\label{def:split-pair}
Let \(q:X\to Q\) be a source quotient, \(F:X\to Y\) a map, and
\(r:Y\to R\) a target identification.  The \emph{split-pair
obstruction} is
\[
  \Delta(q,F,r)
  =
  \{(x,x')\in X\times X
    \mid q(x)=q(x')\ \text{and}\ rF(x)\ne rF(x')\}.
\]
It is the set of pairs identified by the source quotient but separated
after transport to the target quotient.

conclusion: q_I factors through pi
expanded_source_wording_tex:
\label{thm:F10}
Let \(\sigma_I:H\to\Sigma\) be an observation signature with access
quotient \(q_I:H\to Q_I\).  Every observable \(o:H\to R\) that
is constant on access classes factors uniquely through
\(q_I\):
\[
  o=\overline o\circ q_I
\]
for a unique \(\overline o:Q_I\to R\).  Moreover, \(Q_I\) is the
coarsest quotient carrying the declared observations: if
\(\pi:H\to Q'\) is any quotient whose fibers are observation-invisible,
then \(q_I\) factors through \(\pi\).

\label{thm:F10}
Let \(\obsSig:H\to\Sigma\) be an observation signature with access
quotient \(\accessQ:H\to Q_I\).  Every observable \(o:H\to R\) that
is constant on access classes factors uniquely through
\(\accessQ\):
\[
  o=\overline o\circ \accessQ
\]
for a unique \(\overline o:Q_I\to R\).  Moreover, \(Q_I\) is the
coarsest quotient carrying the declared observations: if
\(\pi:H\to Q'\) is any quotient whose fibers are observation-invisible,
then \(\accessQ\) factors through \(\pi\).

\label{thm:F12}

produce a strict new current distinction.  If a readout

the distinction requires declared memory data, bridge data, residual
budget, scope change, or an enlarged calibration family.

\begin{definition}[Hiddenness interface]\label{def:hiddenness-exposure}
A \emph{hiddenness interface} \(I\) consists of a closure carrier
\(\mathcal H_I\), a current quotient
\(\currQ_I:\mathcal H_I\to Q_I\), a predictive quotient
\(\predM_I:\mathcal H_I\to M_I\) refining \(\currQ_I\), and the
following predicates:
\[
  \operatorname{determiningStateTyped}(I),\quad
  \operatorname{minimalRelevantUpstream}(I),\quad
  \operatorname{lawfulCurrentExposure}(I),
\]
together with
\[
  \operatorname{QuotientExposed}(I),\quad
  \operatorname{PredictiveCollapse}(I),\quad
  \operatorname{PredictiveSurplus}(I),\quad
  \operatorname{HiddenFromCurrent}(I).
\]
The hidden-from-current predicate records that one current fiber
contains at least two predictive classes.  The quotient-exposed
predicate records that the lawful exposure quotient removes exactly
those predictive splits.  The hiddenness normal form is the
five-conjunct property
\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{HiddennessNormalForm}(I)
  :={}&
  \operatorname{determiningStateTyped}(I)
  \wedge
  \operatorname{minimalRelevantUpstream}(I)\\
  &{}\wedge
  \bigl(\operatorname{lawfulCurrentExposure}(I)
    \leftrightarrow
    \operatorname{QuotientExposed}(I)\bigr)\\
  &{}\wedge
  \bigl(\operatorname{PredictiveCollapse}(I)
    \leftrightarrow
    \operatorname{lawfulCurrentExposure}(I)\bigr)\\
  &{}\wedge
  \bigl(\operatorname{PredictiveSurplus}(I)
    \leftrightarrow
    \operatorname{HiddenFromCurrent}(I)\bigr).
\end{align*}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Hiddenness Normal Form]\label{thm:F13a}
Let \(I\) be a hiddenness interface and let
\[
  \mathsf{src}:
  \operatorname{Paper7SaturatedSATInstance}(I)
\]
be the opaque saturated-SAT source certificate.  Then
\begin{align*}
  &\operatorname{determiningStateTyped}(I),\\
  &\operatorname{minimalRelevantUpstream}(I),\\
  &\operatorname{lawfulCurrentExposure}(I)
    \iff \operatorname{QuotientExposed}(I),\\
  &\operatorname{PredictiveCollapse}(I)
    \iff \operatorname{lawfulCurrentExposure}(I),\\
  &\operatorname{PredictiveSurplus}(I)
    \iff \operatorname{HiddenFromCurrent}(I).
\end{align*}
That is, \(I\) satisfies
\(\operatorname{HiddennessNormalForm}(I)\).
\end{theorem}
\footnote{The Lean theorem at
\texttt{Access.HiddennessNormalForm.hiddenness\_normal\_form}
proves the layer-agnostic statement under a substrate-pending axiom
\texttt{hiddenness\_pending} guarded by an opaque source predicate;
the substrate proof appears in \citep{Tsiokos2026PvNP} and will
discharge the axiom when its Lean ships.  See
\Cref{app:formalization} for the narrowing disclosure.}
\begin{proof}
Apply the same-paper substrate-pending axiom
\(\mathrm{hiddenness\_pending}\), specialized to the hiddenness
interface \(I\) under the saturated-SAT source certificate \(\mathsf{src}\).
The axiom delivers the conjunction
\[
  \operatorname{HiddennessNormalForm}(I),
\]
that is, the five displayed conjuncts in the statement:
\begin{align*}
  &\operatorname{determiningStateTyped}(I),\qquad
  \operatorname{minimalRelevantUpstream}(I),\\
  &\operatorname{lawfulCurrentExposure}(I)
    \iff \operatorname{QuotientExposed}(I),\\
  &\operatorname{PredictiveCollapse}(I)
    \iff \operatorname{lawfulCurrentExposure}(I),\\
  &\operatorname{PredictiveSurplus}(I)
    \iff \operatorname{HiddenFromCurrent}(I).
\end{align*}
The substrate-side proof of the axiom lives in the saturated-SAT
analysis of \citet{Tsiokos2026PvNP}; within this paper the
wrapper records the layer-agnostic conjunction as the hiddenness
normal form.  The opacity-guard pattern of \Cref{sec:apparatus}
ensures that no instantiation of \(\mathrm{hiddenness\_pending}\) can
derive \(\mathrm{False}\) from the axiom alone: the guard
\(\operatorname{Paper7SaturatedSATInstance}\) has no public
constructor, so an actual instance must come from the saturated-SAT
substrate Lean.
\end{proof}

the PvNP paper \citep{Tsiokos2026PvNP}, and it does not assert any
conclusion about a specific computational complexity class.  It
records the layer-agnostic access law: hiddenness means that a
predictive distinction exists upstream of current access, and
exposure is the minimal quotient refinement that removes that gap.

hidden-variable obstruction is the Kochen--Specker theorem
\citep{KochenSpecker1967Hidden}; that is a substrate-specific
result, not a special case of the layer-agnostic law above.

\label{thm:F13b}
Let \(\mathsf{FPC}\) be the class of formed predictive closures
\(\mathcal C\), each carrying a hiddenness interface with current
quotient \(Q\) and predictive quotient \(M\), together with
four declared side-condition predicates
\begin{align*}
  &\operatorname{genuinelyFormed}(\mathcal C),\qquad
  \operatorname{saturatedCurrentizers}(\mathcal C),\\
  &\operatorname{determiningStateDeclared}(\mathcal C),\qquad
  \operatorname{sourceReadoutSeparated}(\mathcal C).
\end{align*}
Write
\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{FormedClosureReady}(\mathcal C)
  :={}&
  \operatorname{genuinelyFormed}(\mathcal C)
  \wedge\operatorname{saturatedCurrentizers}(\mathcal C)\\
  &{}\wedge\operatorname{determiningStateDeclared}(\mathcal C)
  \wedge\operatorname{sourceReadoutSeparated}(\mathcal C).
\end{align*}
Let \(\operatorname{CSLSrc}:\mathsf{FPC}\to\mathrm{Prop}\) be the
opaque CSL diagnosis-source predicate.
Then for every \(\mathcal C\in\mathsf{FPC}\),
\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{CSLSrc}(\mathcal C)
  \Longrightarrow{}&
    \operatorname{FormedClosureReady}(\mathcal C)\\
  \Longrightarrow{}&
    \bigl(
      \operatorname{PredictiveSurplus}(\mathcal C)
      \iff
      \operatorname{HiddenFromCurrent}(\mathcal C)
    \bigr).
\end{align*}
Here \(\operatorname{PredictiveSurplus}\) and
\(\operatorname{HiddenFromCurrent}\) are the predictive-surplus and
hidden-from-current predicates of \Cref{def:hiddenness-exposure}.  In
a formed predictive closure with the CSL diagnosis source and the
four declared side conditions, predictive surplus across the
\(M/Q\) gap survives exactly when the determining state is
hidden from current observation.

\label{thm:F6}
Let \(\mathcal P\) be a formed stability package with a
layer-dissolving membrane.  Suppose \(\mathcal P\) declares:
\begin{itemize}
  \item a currency block \(C\) on its exterior carrier of size \(e\);
  \item a layer-bridge block \(L\) of size \(y\times e\) and a
  dissolving-direction block \(D\) of size \(z\times e\), with block
  currency pieces \(K_{LL}\), \(K_{LD}\), \(K_{DL}\), and \(K_{DD}\);
  \item the symmetry conditions \(K_{DL}=K_{LD}^{\!\top}\) and
  \(K_{LL}^{\dagger}=(K_{LL}^{\dagger})^{\!\top}\), together with the
  Moore--Penrose projection identity
  \[
    K_{LL}\,K_{LL}^{\dagger}\,K_{LD}=K_{LD};
  \]
  \item currency and residual budgets
  \[
    K_{LL}\preceq \Theta_Y,
    \qquad
    \Xi(C,L,D,K_{LL}^{\dagger})\preceq \Omega_Z,
  \]
  where \(\Xi\) is the adequacy residual;
  \item a transport selector \(S\) of size \(d\times z\) satisfying
  the endpoint budget
  \[
    S\bigl(\widehat E\,\Theta_Y\,\widehat E^{\!\top}
      +\Omega_Z\bigr)S^{\!\top}\preceq\Theta_D,
  \]
  where \(\widehat E\) is the optimal native explanation determined
  by \((C,L,D,K_{LL}^{\dagger})\).
\end{itemize}
Then the transported dissolving block satisfies the Loewner endpoint
\[
  S\,K_{DD}\,S^{\!\top}\preceq\Theta_D .
\]
Equivalently, every layer-dissolving move accepted by \(\mathcal P\)
is bounded by its declared transport budget; no unpriced
layer-dissolving needle survives the formed package.

expanded_source_wording_tex:
The first transport law is the quotient descent criterion already
introduced in \Cref{sec:intro}.  We use the split-pair obstruction of
\Cref{def:split-pair}.

\begin{definition}[Canonical target-repair quotient]\label{def:target-repair}
Let \(q:X\to Q\), \(F:X\to Y\), and \(r:Y\to R\).  The canonical
target-repair relation \(\equiv_F\) on \(R\) is the smallest
equivalence relation generated by the identifications
\[
  r(Fx)\equiv_F r(Fx')
  \qquad\text{whenever}\qquad
  q(x)=q(x').
\]
The \emph{canonical target-repair quotient} is
\[
  R_F:=R/{\equiv_F},
\]
with quotient map \(c_F:R\to R_F\).
\end{definition}

\label{thm:F2}
Let \(q:X\to Q\) be a quotient map, let \(F:X\to Y\) be a map, and
let \(r:Y\to R\) be a target readout.  Then \(r\circ F\) descends
through \(q\) if and only if

refinement, which separates the offending source fibers, and target
coarsening by the quotient \(c_F:R\to R_F\) of
\Cref{def:target-repair}.  The target repair is minimal among target
coarsenings that make \(r\circ F\) descend.

The second transport law concerns route dependence: two routes can be
indistinguishable at the current quotient while still leaving a

\begin{definition}[Route residue]\label{def:route-residue}
Let \(H\) be a carrier, let \(\gamma,\eta:H\to Z\) be two declared
routes, let \(Q:Z\to Q\) be the current quotient, and let
\(M:Z\to M\) be a predictive quotient refining the current
readout.  The \emph{route residue} of \(\gamma\) and \(\eta\) at
\(h\in H\) is present when
\[
  Q(\gamma h)=Q(\eta h)
  \quad\text{but}\quad
  M(\gamma h)\neM(\eta h).
\]
\end{definition}

\label{thm:F3}
For two declared routes \(\gamma,\eta:H\to Z\), current quotient
\(Q\), and predictive quotient \(M\), memory is forced
exactly when there is route residue.  Equivalently, if two route
outputs agree at \(Q\) but differ at \(M\), then no
representation through the current quotient alone is sufficient for
the declared future probes.  Recording the route residue gives the
canonical memory repair.

source_wording_tex:
\label{thm:F3}
For two declared routes \(\gamma,\eta:H\to Z\), current quotient
\(\currQ\), and predictive quotient \(\predM\), memory is forced
exactly when there is route residue.  Equivalently, if two route
outputs agree at \(\currQ\) but differ at \(\predM\), then no
representation through the current quotient alone is sufficient for
the declared future probes.  Recording the route residue gives the
canonical memory repair.

expanded_source_wording_tex:
The third transport law is the local-to-global image criterion.  It
separates overlap tests from genuine global existence.

\begin{definition}[Local-global compatibility]\label{def:local-global-compat}
Let \(I\) index a declared finite patch system, with local object sets
\((Q_i)_{i\in I}\).  Let \(\mathcal C\subseteq \prod_i Q_i\) be the
subset of local families satisfying all declared overlap comparisons.
Let \(Q\) be the global object set and
\[
  R:Q\to \prod_i Q_i
\]
the declared restriction map.  A local family \(a\in\prod_i Q_i\) is
\emph{compatible} if \(a\in\mathcal C\), and it \emph{globalizes} if
\(a\in\operatorname{im}(R)\).
\end{definition}

expanded_source_wording_tex:
\label{thm:F4}
Let \(\mathcal G\) be a set of global states, let \(\mathcal F\) be a
set of local-family data, let
\(\operatorname{Comp}:\mathcal F\to\mathrm{Prop}\) be the
overlap-compatibility predicate, and let
\[
  R:\mathcal G\longrightarrow\mathcal F
\]
be a declared restriction map such that
\(\operatorname{Comp}(R(g))\) for every \(g\in\mathcal G\).  For
\(a\in\mathcal F\), write
\[
  \operatorname{Globalizes}_R(a)
  \quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \exists g\in\mathcal G,\ R(g)=a.
\]
Then
\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{Comp}(a)
  &\Longrightarrow
  \bigl(\operatorname{Globalizes}_R(a)
  \iff a\in R(\mathcal G)\bigr),\\
  \operatorname{ExactlyOneStatus}(a)
  &\iff
  \operatorname{OverlapInconsistent}(a)
  \mathbin{\dot\vee}
  \operatorname{CompatibleNonGlobal}(a)\\
  &\hspace{3.5em}\mathbin{\dot\vee}
  \operatorname{GloballyAmbiguous}(a)
  \mathbin{\dot\vee}
  \operatorname{GloballyExact}(a),
\end{align*}
where the four status predicates are determined by
\(\operatorname{Comp}(a)\), membership in \(R(\mathcal G)\), and the
cardinality of the fiber \(R^{-1}(a)\).

expanded_source_wording_tex:
\label{thm:F5}
Let \(K:B\to Q_K\) be a branchwise quotient and
\(R:B\to Q_R\) a recombination quotient on the same branch carrier.
Then branchwise equality determines recombination equality if and only
if \(R\) factors through \(K\), that is, if and only if there exists
\(\rho:Q_K\to Q_R\) such that
\[
  R=\rho\circ K .
\]
Equivalently, the branch-merge split-pair obstruction of
\Cref{def:bridge-composition} is empty.

\label{def:involutive-ledger}
An involutive ledger is a carrier \(X\) equipped with an involution
\(J:X\to X\), so \(J^2=\mathrm{id}\).  Its fixed locus is
\[
  \mathrm{Fix}(J)=\{x\in X:J(x)=x\}.
\]
An anti-invariant readout is a quantity whose sign changes under
\(J\).  It is separating when zero trace against the
anti-invariant readout forces the corresponding visible
anti-invariant mass to vanish.

\begin{definition}[Selection obstruction]\label{def:selection-obstruction}
Let a declared symmetry group \(G\) act on a carrier \(X\), and let
\[
  p:X\to X/G
\]
be the orbit quotient.  For a selectedness predicate
\(\chi:X\to\{0,1\}\), the selection obstruction is the split-pair set
\[
  \Delta(p,\chi)
  =
  \{(x,x')\in X\times X:
      p(x)=p(x')\ \text{and}\ \chi(x)\ne\chi(x')\}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Selection Obstruction / Repair Normal Form]\label{thm:F15a}
Let \(G\) act on a set \(X\) and on an orbit set \(O\) by
\(\rho_X:G\times X\to X\) and \(\rho_O:G\times O\to O\).  Let
\(\pi:X\to O\) be a surjective orbit map, let
\(s:X\to\{0,1\}\) be a selectedness predicate, let
\(\sigma:O\to X\) be a section, and let \(b:X\to B\) be a breaker
readout.  Define
\[
  \mathcal O_s
  :=
  \{(x,x')\in X^2:\pi(x)=\pi(x')\ \text{and}\ s(x)\ne s(x')\}.
\]
Then
\begin{align*}
  &\operatorname{EquivariantSelector}(\rho_O,\rho_X,\sigma)
    \wedge \operatorname{TrivialOrbitAction}(\rho_O)\\
  &\hspace{4em}\Longrightarrow
    \forall o\in O,\ \forall g\in G,\
      \rho_X(g,\sigma(o))=\sigma(o),\\
  s\ \text{descends through}\ \pi
  &\iff
  \mathcal O_s=\emptyset
  \iff
  \exists\,\bar s:O\to\{0,1\}\ \text{with}\ \bar s\circ\pi=s,\\
  \operatorname{HasSelectionSplit}(\pi,s)
  &\iff
  \mathcal O_s\ne\emptyset.
\end{align*}
Thus an equivariant selector can select only common fixed points
unless a declared breaker \(b\), memory, condition, or quotient
refinement supplies additional data.
\end{theorem}
\footnote{Verified in Lean as
\texttt{Symmetry.SelectionObstruction.selection\_obstruction}; see
\Cref{app:formalization}.}
\begin{proof}
Assume the actions \(\rho_X,\rho_O\), the surjective orbit map
\(\pi\), the selectedness predicate \(s\), and the section
\(\sigma\).  If \(\sigma\) is equivariant and the \(G\)-action on
\(O\) is trivial, then for every \(g\in G\) and \(o\in O\),
\[
  \pi(\rho_X(g,\sigma(o)))
  =
  \rho_O(g,\pi(\sigma(o)))
  =
  \rho_O(g,o)
  =
  o.
\]
Equivariance of the selector gives
\(\rho_X(g,\sigma(o))=\sigma(\rho_O(g,o))=\sigma(o)\), so
\(\sigma(o)\) lies in the common fixed locus of the \(G\)-action on
\(X\).

source_wording_tex:
\begin{definition}[Selection obstruction]\label{def:selection-obstruction}
Let a declared symmetry group \(G\) act on a carrier \(X\), and let
\[
  p:X\to X/G
\]
be the orbit quotient.  For a selectedness predicate
\(\chi:X\to\{0,1\}\), the selection obstruction is the split-pair set
\[
  \splitObs(p,\chi)
  =
  \{(x,x')\in X\times X:
      p(x)=p(x')\ \text{and}\ \chi(x)\ne\chi(x')\}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Selection Obstruction / Repair Normal Form]\label{thm:F15a}
Let \(G\) act on a set \(X\) and on an orbit set \(O\) by
\(\rho_X:G\times X\to X\) and \(\rho_O:G\times O\to O\).  Let
\(\pi:X\to O\) be a surjective orbit map, let
\(s:X\to\{0,1\}\) be a selectedness predicate, let
\(\sigma:O\to X\) be a section, and let \(b:X\to B\) be a breaker
readout.  Define
\[
  \mathcal O_s
  :=
  \{(x,x')\in X^2:\pi(x)=\pi(x')\ \text{and}\ s(x)\ne s(x')\}.
\]
Then
\begin{align*}
  &\operatorname{EquivariantSelector}(\rho_O,\rho_X,\sigma)
    \wedge \operatorname{TrivialOrbitAction}(\rho_O)\\
  &\hspace{4em}\Longrightarrow
    \forall o\in O,\ \forall g\in G,\
      \rho_X(g,\sigma(o))=\sigma(o),\\
  s\ \text{descends through}\ \pi
  &\iff
  \mathcal O_s=\emptyset
  \iff
  \exists\,\bar s:O\to\{0,1\}\ \text{with}\ \bar s\circ\pi=s,\\
  \operatorname{HasSelectionSplit}(\pi,s)
  &\iff
  \mathcal O_s\ne\emptyset.
\end{align*}
Thus an equivariant selector can select only common fixed points
unless a declared breaker \(b\), memory, condition, or quotient
refinement supplies additional data.
\end{theorem}
\footnote{Verified in Lean as
\texttt{Symmetry.SelectionObstruction.selection\_obstruction}; see
\Cref{app:formalization}.}
\begin{proof}
Assume the actions \(\rho_X,\rho_O\), the surjective orbit map
\(\pi\), the selectedness predicate \(s\), and the section
\(\sigma\).  If \(\sigma\) is equivariant and the \(G\)-action on
\(O\) is trivial, then for every \(g\in G\) and \(o\in O\),
\[
  \pi(\rho_X(g,\sigma(o)))
  =
  \rho_O(g,\pi(\sigma(o)))
  =
  \rho_O(g,o)
  =
  o.
\]
Equivariance of the selector gives
\(\rho_X(g,\sigma(o))=\sigma(\rho_O(g,o))=\sigma(o)\), so
\(\sigma(o)\) lies in the common fixed locus of the \(G\)-action on
\(X\).

\label{thm:F15b}
Let \(\mathcal C\) be a closure space with a \(G\)-action, let
\(\Omega:\mathcal C\to\mathrm{Prop}\) be the ground-state predicate,
and let \(\mathcal B=\mathcal C/G\) be the branch quotient.  Suppose
a future branch-selection formation source is given for
\((\mathcal C,G,\Omega)\).  Then there is a formation operator
\[
  F:\mathcal C\longrightarrow\mathcal B
\]
and data \(c\in\mathcal C\), \(g\in G\) such that
\[
  \Omega(c)
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  g\cdot F(c)\ne F(c).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  \exists F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal B,\,
  \exists c\in\mathcal C,\,
  \exists g\in G,\,
  \Omega(c)\wedge g\cdot F(c)\ne F(c).
\]

\label{thm:F40}
Let \(G\) act on a history space \(H\) by
\(\alpha:G\times H\to H\), let \(q:H\to Q\) be a surjective quotient,
let \(\bar\alpha:G\times Q\to Q\) be a candidate descended action,
let \(D:G\times H\to\{0,1\}\) be a domain predicate, and let
\(r:H\to V\) be a readout with value action
\(\rho:G\times V\to V\).  Define
\[
  \mathcal O_{\alpha}
  :=
  \{(g,h,h'):\ q(h)=q(h')\ \text{and}\
    q(\alpha(g,h))\ne q(\alpha(g,h'))\},
\]
and define \(\mathcal O_D\) analogously by replacing
\(q(\alpha(g,h))\) with \(D(g,h)\).  Then
\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{SymmetryDescends}(q,\alpha)
  &\iff \mathcal O_{\alpha}=\emptyset,\\
  \operatorname{DomainDescends}(q,D)
  &\iff \mathcal O_D=\emptyset,\\
  \operatorname{GroupLawPreserved}(\bar\alpha)
  &\iff
  \forall g,g'\in G,\forall \bar h\in Q,\,
    \bar\alpha(gg',\bar h)=
    \bar\alpha(g,\bar\alpha(g',\bar h)),\\
  \operatorname{ReadoutPreserved}(r,\alpha,\rho)
  &\iff
  \forall g\in G,\forall h\in H,\,
    r(\alpha(g,h))=\rho(g,r(h)).
\end{align*}
An anomaly is precisely the failure of at least one of these four
conditions.

\label{thm:F41}
Let \(\mathcal C_A,\mathcal C_B\) be formed closures with quotients
\(q_A:\mathcal C_A\to Q_A\) and \(q_B:\mathcal C_B\to Q_B\).  Let
\(F:\mathcal C_A\to\mathcal C_B\) and
\(G:\mathcal C_B\to\mathcal C_A\) descend to
\(\bar F:Q_A\to Q_B\) and \(\bar G:Q_B\to Q_A\).  Let
\(r_A:R_A\to S_A\), \(r_B:R_B\to S_B\) be role readouts, let
\(\tau:R_A\to R_B\) be role translation, let
\(\rho:S_A\to S_B\) be the role-value map, and let
\(\phi:\mathcal R_A\to\mathcal R_B\) and
\(\kappa:\mathcal K_A\to\mathcal K_B\) translate routes and claims.
Then a role-preserving duality equivalence holds if and only if
\begin{align*}
  \bar G\circ\bar F&=\mathrm{id}_{Q_A}
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \bar F\circ\bar G=\mathrm{id}_{Q_B},\\
  r_B\circ\tau&=\rho\circ r_A,\\
  \bar F\circ R_A(\gamma)
  &=R_B(\phi(\gamma))\circ\bar F
  \quad\forall \gamma\in\mathcal R_A,\\
  \operatorname{status}_B(\kappa(k))
  &=\operatorname{status}_A(k)
  \quad\forall k\in\mathcal K_A.
\end{align*}

\label{thm:F17}
Let \(H\) be a carrier with a family of access quotients
\(q_i:H\to Q_i\) indexed by \(i\in I\), a public quotient
\(p:H\to P\), and a target readout \(r:H\to R\).  Assume each
\(q_i\) is surjective, \(p\) is surjective, and the family satisfies
the common-quotient universal property
\(\operatorname{CommonQuotientUniversal}(q,p)\): \(p\) factors
through every \(q_i\), and any quotient through which all \(q_i\)
factor also factors through \(p\).  Then
\begin{align*}
  &\operatorname{CommonAcrossAccesses}(q,r)
    \iff \operatorname{PublicDeterminesObject}(p,r),\\
  &\operatorname{CommonAcrossAccesses}(q,r)\\
  &\qquad{}\iff
    \forall i\in I,\,
      \operatorname{AccessObjectivityDefectEmpty}(q_i,r),\\
  &\operatorname{PublicDeterminesObject}(p,r)\\
  &\qquad{}\iff
    \operatorname{ObstructionEmpty}
      \bigl(\operatorname{PublicToObjectDefect}(p,r)\bigr),
\end{align*}
together with
\begin{align*}
  &\operatorname{CommonQuotientVisible}(q,p),\\
  &\operatorname{RetainsPublicQuotient}
      \bigl(p,\operatorname{objectiveExtension}(p,r)\bigr),\\
  &\operatorname{CarriesObject}
      \bigl(\operatorname{objectiveExtension}(p,r),r\bigr),
\end{align*}
and the status partition
\[
  \operatorname{ExactlyOneObjectivityStatus}(p,r).
\]

\label{thm:F19}
Let \(H_i,H_j\) be carriers with access quotients
\(q_i:H_i\to Q_i\) and \(q_j:H_j\to Q_j\), and let
\(\gamma:H_i\to H_j\) be a declared transport.  Assume \(q_i\) and
\(q_j\) are surjective.  Let
\(\operatorname{viable}:Q_j\to\mathrm{Prop}\) be a viability
predicate, \(C:H_i\times H_j\to\mathrm{Prop}\) a relation predicate,
and let
\[
  \bar\gamma:Q_i\to Q_j,\qquad
  \bar\eta:Q_j\to Q_k,\qquad
  \operatorname{compBar}:Q_i\to Q_k
\]
be arbitrary holonomy data (no compatibility between
\(\operatorname{compBar}\) and \(\bar\eta\circ\bar\gamma\) is
assumed).  Then
\begin{align*}
  &\operatorname{Persists}(q_i,\gamma,q_j)
    \iff
    \operatorname{PersistenceObstructionEmpty}(q_i,\gamma,q_j),\\
  &\operatorname{SplitObstructionEmpty}(q_i,\gamma,q_j)
    \iff
    \operatorname{Persists}(q_i,\gamma,q_j),\\
  &\operatorname{ViablePersistence}(\gamma,q_j,\operatorname{viable})
    \iff
    \operatorname{DissolutionObstructionEmpty}
      (\gamma,q_j,\operatorname{viable}),\\
  &\operatorname{RelationValuedPersistence}(q_i,q_j,C)
    \iff
    \operatorname{RelationPersistenceObstructionEmpty}(q_i,q_j,C),\\
  &\operatorname{IdentityHolonomyCoherent}
      (\bar\gamma,\bar\eta,\operatorname{compBar})\\
  &\qquad{}\iff
    \operatorname{IdentityHolonomyDefectEmpty}
      (\bar\gamma,\bar\eta,\operatorname{compBar}),
\end{align*}
together with the comparison-status partition
\[
  \operatorname{ExactlyOnePersistenceComparisonStatus}
    (q_i,\gamma,q_j),
\]
and the retention and carrying conditions
\begin{align*}
  &\operatorname{RetainsOldIdentity}
      \bigl(q_i,\operatorname{persistenceExtension}(q_i,\gamma,q_j)\bigr),\\
  &\operatorname{CarriesLaterIdentity}
      \bigl(\operatorname{persistenceExtension}(q_i,\gamma,q_j),
        \gamma,q_j\bigr).
\end{align*}

\label{thm:F20}
Let \(H_0,H_1,H_s,H_t\) be history spaces with event readout
\(\varepsilon:H_0\to E\), continuation \(\gamma:H_0\to H_1\),
record readouts
\[
  \rho_1:H_1\to R_1,\qquad
  \rho_s:H_s\to R_s,\qquad
  \rho_t:H_t\to R_t,
\]
transport \(\theta:H_s\to H_t\), descended transport
\(\bar\theta:R_s\to R_t\), fact-value maps
\(d_s:R_s\to E_s\), \(d_t:R_t\to E_t\), update
\(u:E_s\to E_t\), and a packaging map \(C:H\to H\) on an auxiliary
carrier \(H\).  Define the record signature
\[
  s:=\rho_1\circ\gamma:H_0\to R_1,
\]
and assume that \(s\) and \(\rho_s\) are surjective.  Define
\begin{align*}
  \mathcal O_{\mathrm{ev}}
  &:=
  \{(h,h')\in H_0^2:
      \rho_1(\gamma h)=\rho_1(\gamma h')
      \text{ and } \varepsilon(h)\ne\varepsilon(h')\},\\
  \mathcal O_{\mathrm{red}}
  &:=
  \{(h,h')\in H_0^2:
      \varepsilon(h)=\varepsilon(h')
      \text{ and } \rho_1(\gamma h)\ne\rho_1(\gamma h')\},\\
  \mathcal O_{\mathrm{rec}}
  &:=
  \{(x,y)\in H_s^2:
      \rho_s(x)=\rho_s(y)
      \text{ and } \rho_t(\theta x)\ne\rho_t(\theta y)\},\\
  \mathcal O_{\mathrm{val}}
  &:=
  \{r\in R_s:
      d_t(\bar\theta r)\ne u(d_s r)\}.
\end{align*}
Then
\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{EventRecorded}(\varepsilon,\gamma,\rho_1)
  &\iff \mathcal O_{\mathrm{ev}}=\emptyset,\\
  \operatorname{RecordStable}(\rho_s,\theta,\rho_t)
  &\iff \mathcal O_{\mathrm{rec}}=\emptyset,\\
  \operatorname{FactValueStable}(\bar\theta,d_s,d_t,u)
  &\iff \mathcal O_{\mathrm{val}}=\emptyset,\\
  \operatorname{StableFact}
  &\iff
  \mathcal O_{\mathrm{ev}}=\emptyset
  \wedge
  \mathcal O_{\mathrm{rec}}=\emptyset
  \wedge
  \mathcal O_{\mathrm{val}}=\emptyset.
\end{align*}
together with the record-comparison status partition
\[
  \operatorname{ExactlyOneRecordComparisonStatus}
    (\varepsilon,\gamma,\rho_1),
\]
the retention and carrying conditions for the record-event extension
\(\langle\rho_1\circ\gamma,\varepsilon\rangle:H_0\to R_1\times E\),
\begin{align*}
  &\operatorname{RetainsRecord}
      \bigl(\rho_1\circ\gamma,
        \langle\rho_1\circ\gamma,\varepsilon\rangle\bigr),\\
  &\operatorname{CarriesEvent}
      \bigl(\langle\rho_1\circ\gamma,\varepsilon\rangle,
        \varepsilon\bigr),
\end{align*}
and the idempotent-packaging fixed-point property
\[
  \operatorname{IdempotentPackaging}(C)
  \Longrightarrow
  \forall h\in H,\ C(C(h))=C(h).
\]
The record-comparison status takes one of four values
(\emph{exact}, \emph{redundant}, \emph{ambiguous}, or
\emph{incomparable}) determined by the joint emptiness pattern of
\(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{ev}}\) and \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{red}}\).

For every c∈ C , SelfCertificationBlocked_ pi (c), AcceptedScopedLowerAudit_ pi (c) implies _ pi (c), HasMetaLayerCertificate_ mu (c) implies m∈ M, Audits_ mu (m,c) _ pi (c), CompleteSelfSoundness_ pi (c) implies OutsideScope_ pi (c).
expanded_source_wording_tex:
\label{thm:F21}
Let \(\mathcal C\) be a space of claims, let
\(\pi\) be a same-layer audit policy on \(\mathcal C\), and let
\(\mu\) be a meta-layer audit relation from \(\mathcal C\) to a
space \(\mathcal M\) of meta-claims.  For every
\(c\in\mathcal C\),
\begin{align*}
  &\operatorname{SelfCertificationBlocked}_{\pi}(c),\\
  &\operatorname{AcceptedScopedLowerAudit}_{\pi}(c)
    \Longrightarrow
    \neg\operatorname{CompleteSelfSoundness}_{\pi}(c),\\
  &\operatorname{HasMetaLayerCertificate}_{\mu}(c)
    \Longrightarrow
    \exists m\in\mathcal M,\,
      \operatorname{Audits}_{\mu}(m,c)
      \wedge
      \neg\operatorname{SelfSound}_{\pi}(c),\\
  &\operatorname{CompleteSelfSoundness}_{\pi}(c)
    \Longrightarrow
    \operatorname{OutsideScope}_{\pi}(c).
\end{align*}

expanded_source_wording_tex:
There are two cases for a legitimate reflexive audit.  In the
same-layer case, the previous paragraph blocks complete
self-soundness.  In the meta-layer case, a certificate supplies
\(m\in\mathcal M\) with
\[
  \operatorname{Audits}_{\mu}(m,c)
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \neg\operatorname{SelfSound}_{\pi}(c),
\]
so the audit has moved to a strict meta-layer.  Therefore any claim
of complete same-layer self-soundness lies outside the scope of
\(\pi\).
\end{proof}

conclusion: Complete self-attestation by the issuer is outside the scope of the regime .
expanded_source_wording_tex:
\item[\emph{Sarbanes-Oxley independent-audit mandate
(corporate-finance regulation).}]
The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 forbids public-company
financial statements from being audited by the issuer's
own accounting staff.  Management's internal-controls
assessment under \S404(a) is the scoped lower audit; the
independent CPA firm's attestation under \S404(b) is the
meta-layer certificate, and the auditor is itself
overseen by the Public Company Accounting Oversight
Board, producing a tower of meta-audits.  Complete
self-attestation by the issuer is outside the scope of
the regime \citep{SarbanesOxley2002Act}.

conclusion: Complete in-certificate self-trust is outside the scope of the protocol .
expanded_source_wording_tex:
\item[\emph{X.509 PKI external root-of-trust
(cryptographic protocol design).}]
In the X.509 public-key infrastructure, an endpoint
certificate cannot self-certify its trustworthiness to a
relying party: validation requires a chain of signatures
terminating at a root certificate authority in the
client's externally maintained trust store, which acts
as the meta-layer.  The leaf's own self-signature and
local syntactic integrity checks are the scoped lower
audit; self-signed leaves are rejected by default by
mainstream TLS clients.  Complete in-certificate
self-trust is outside the scope of the protocol
\citep{Cooper2008RFC5280}.

expanded_source_wording_tex:
\label{thm:F22}
Let \(q:X\to Q\) be a source quotient, let
\(\beta:Y\to B\) be a boundary readout, let
\(U:X\times Y\to X'\) be an interface update, and let
\(q':X'\to Q'\) be the target quotient.  Assume \(q\), \(\beta\),
and \(q'\) are surjective.  Define
\[
  \mathcal O_U
  :=
  \{((x,y),(x',y')) :
    q(x)=q(x'),\ \beta(y)=\beta(y'),\
    q'(U(x,y))\ne q'(U(x',y'))\}.
\]
Then
\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{InterfaceMediated}(q,\beta,U,q')
  &\iff \mathcal O_U=\emptyset\\
  &\iff
  \exists\,\bar U:Q\times B\to Q'\ \text{with}\
    \bar U(q(x),\beta(y))=q'(U(x,y))\ \forall x,y,\\
  \mathcal O_U=\emptyset
  &\Longrightarrow
  \operatorname{BoundaryLeakageAbsent}\wedge
  \operatorname{InternalInsufficiencyAbsent},\\
  \operatorname{ActiveMediatedInfluence}(\bar U)

\[

\]

\begin{align*}
  r\ \text{descends through}\ q

  &\iff

  \wedge

\end{align*}

\label{thm:F25}
Let \(q:H\to Q\) be a context quotient, let
\(\alpha:A\to\bar A\) be an intervention abstraction, let
\(\Gamma:H\times A\to H'\) be an intervention transport, let
\(r:H'\to R\) be a target readout, and let
\(K:H\times A\to K_0\) be a kernel outcome.  Let
\(\operatorname{Adm}:Q\times\bar A\to\mathrm{Prop}\) and let
\(\operatorname{ResStable}\) and
\(\operatorname{ProbResStable}\) be residue-stability predicates.
Define
\[
  \mathcal O_{\Gamma}
  :=
  \{((h,a),(h',a')) :
    q(h)=q(h'),\ \alpha(a)=\alpha(a'),\
    r(\Gamma(h,a))\ne r(\Gamma(h',a'))\}.
\]
Write \(\operatorname{ITD}\), \(\operatorname{PITD}\), and
\(\operatorname{Caus}\) for the intervention-transport descent,
probabilistic intervention-transport descent, and causal-relation
predicates for this data.  Then
\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{ITD}(q,\alpha,\Gamma,r)
  &\iff \mathcal O_{\Gamma}=\emptyset\\
  &\iff
  \exists\,\bar\Gamma:Q\times\bar A\to R,\
    \bar\Gamma(q(h),\alpha(a))=r(\Gamma(h,a))\ \forall h,a,\\
  \operatorname{PITD}(q,\alpha,K)
  &\iff
  \begin{gathered}
    \exists\,\bar K:Q\times\bar A\to K_0,\
    \bar K(q(h),\alpha(a))=K(h,a)\ \forall h,a,\\
    \operatorname{ProbResStable}(q(h),\alpha(a),\alpha(a'))
  \end{gathered}\\
  \operatorname{Caus}(q,\alpha,\Gamma,r)
  &\iff
  \begin{gathered}
    \operatorname{Adm}\wedge
    \operatorname{ITD}(q,\alpha,\Gamma,r)\\
    {}\wedge\operatorname{ResStable}.
  \end{gathered}
\end{align*}

\(\operatorname{Lawful}:\mathcal C\to\mathrm{Prop}\), equivalence relation
\(\sim\) on lawful closures, moduli quotient
\(p:\mathcal C\to M\), readout \(r:\mathcal C\to V\), transport

\begin{align*}

  \operatorname{NontrivialModuli}(\operatorname{Lawful},\sim)

  \operatorname{NecessaryReadout}(r)

    \operatorname{Lawful}(c)\wedge\operatorname{Lawful}(d)

\end{align*}

\label{thm:F29}
Let \(P\) be a presentation space with quotient
\(\pi:P\to\Pi\), let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation compatible
with \(\pi\), let \(s:\Pi\to P\) be a section with
\(\pi(s(x))=x\), and let \(T:P\to V\) be a readout.  Let
\(\tau:\operatorname{Tuple}(P)\to\operatorname{Tuple}(\Pi)\) be the
tuple quotient, let \(R:\operatorname{Tuple}(P)\to\mathrm{Prop}\) be a
relation, and let a group \(G\) act on \(P\) and \(V\).  Then
\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{PresentationInvariant}(\pi,T)
  &\iff
  \forall p,p'\in P,\ \pi(p)=\pi(p')\Rightarrow T(p)=T(p')\\
  &\iff
  \exists\,\bar T:\Pi\to V\ \text{with}\ \bar T\circ\pi=T,\\
  \operatorname{EquivalentPresentationInvariant}(\sim,T)
  &\iff
  \forall p,p'\in P,\ p\sim p'\Rightarrow T(p)=T(p'),\\
  \operatorname{PresentationRelationInvariant}(\tau,R)
  &\iff
  \forall x,y,\ \tau(x)=\tau(y)\Rightarrow (R(x)\leftrightarrow R(y)),\\
  \operatorname{GroupEquivariant}(T)
  &\iff
  \forall g\in G,\forall p\in P,\ T(g\cdot p)=g\cdot T(p).
\end{align*}
